youtube.title: Your Eye Isn't Better Than Your Camera. It Cheats.
youtube.description:
Dynamic range is the span from the darkest to the brightest detail you can record, measured in stops (each stop = double the light). With the eye held on one spot, most estimates put human vision at about 10–14 stops (Cambridge in Colour; Wikipedia). A Nikon D850 measured 14.8 EV in DxOMark's landscape (dynamic range) test — the same league. Sunny scenes with deep shade can span 12+ stops (Cambridge in Colour), so one exposure has to throw away the highlights or the shadows.

The eye 'cheats': the pupil adjusts, you look around the scene, and the brain combines those views — with adaptation, up to roughly 24 stops (Cambridge in Colour). Your camera can do the same with bracketing and HDR merging.

Simulation (numpy, computed scene, no photos): a dark archway looking out at a sunny valley spans 14.6 stops; with a 12-stop exposure window, exposing for the shadows clips 16% of the frame to pure white, exposing for the sky crushes 64% to black.

Sources: Cambridge in Colour (Dynamic Range; Cameras vs the Human Eye), Wikipedia (Dynamic range; Multi-exposure HDR capture), Imaging Resource on DxOMark's D850 test, Photography Mad (definition of a stop).
